articles.title: Exclusive’: The hi-fi industry has lost some of its mojo’ — The new boss of Q Acoustics, QED and Goldring explains why bringing Japan’s ‘kissa’ listening cafes to other countries is key to the future of hi-fi, and why it’s so hard for classic manufacturers to compete in the soundbar world
articles.text:
Exclusive: ‘Young people are obsessed by music, but no one's talking to them’ — the new boss of Q Acoustics, QED, and Goldring has plans to give hi-fi its ‘mojo’ back, and it involves opening more ‘kissa’-style listening cafes and ditching Led Zeppelin
Charlie Henderson's background includes Naim and Cambridge Audio, and he's got big plans for refreshing his latest hi-fi charge
You may not have heard of the Armour Home Group, but you have almost certainly heard of its three hi-fi brands: Q Acoustics, QED, and Goldring. Q Acoustics is one of the masters of great-value value speakers, QED is one of the best-known cable makers, and Goldring is a 120-year-old turntable specialist.
And you may not have heard of its new Managing Director, Charlie Henderson, but you will absolutely have heard of the audio brands he's helped to lead, including Cambridge Audio, Naim, and Jabra.
I've met Henderson before in his roles at Cambridge and Naim, and I was fascinated by how the email I received announcing his appointment promised to focus on expanding the brands "beyond the hi-fi" sector.
I wondered if that meant moving into more 'mainstream' parts of the audio world, and I wasn't sure how that would really work with a brand like QED, so I wanted to find out more — but it turned out that Henderson had something completely different in mind.
He wanted to talk about how the brands can support the return of public listening rooms, how they can engage with the new wave of people getting into hi-fi — and how the hi-fi world can get its "mojo" back.
TechRadar: You said in your introduction at the company that "My goal is to elevate these brands beyond the hi-fi sector and into the broader music community", referring to Q Acoustics, QED, and Goldring. So what do you have in mind?
Charlie Henderson: I have felt for a long time that the hi-fi industry has lost some of its mojo. If we go back to the '50s, '60s, '70s — kind of the essence of British hi-fi in particular — lots of those company founders were either part of rock bands, or they were gigging, or they were visiting live venues, and that's why they got into this industry. So a real love of music was always there.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I think we've seen maybe over the last 10 years or so that it's gone a bit stale. And I think in all the roles I've had in this industry, I've been really keen to make sure that we reboot it. So we talk about our mission as a business, which is to move beyond the hi-fi bubble and become part of music culture — almost as though that's revolutionary, but it's not; it's just going back to what hi-fi was. It was always part of music culture.
But if we think about going around Vienna High End or the Bristol Hi-Fi Show or any of these kinds of events, it's usually less about the music and it's mostly about the equipment and the technology. I think that's a shame. It's not why I'm in this industry; it's not why all the people I tend to find that I'm working with are in this industry.
So that is our mission, and the way we do it is by just being authentic about why we're really here.
TR: It's funny, of all the big tech shows, IFA is the one that has started doing what you're saying, and trying to be a cultural hub as well as a tech show. But really audio is such a kind of tangential part of IFA compared to these music shows that you're talking about.
CH: I remember chatting to a [very respected] hi-fi journalist at the Munich show a couple of years ago, and he just hung out with us. This was in my Cambridge [Audio] days, he just kind of just hung out because he was like, 'Man, at least someone's playing some proper music.'
You walk around the halls and it's Kate Bush and Pink Floyd and Led Zeppelin and all of the usual stuff. Great artists, they're still important musical acts and incredible — but decades have moved on and there's different artists today, you know? People like Fred Again and Ren are my two favorites at the moment, because I think they're British artists who are defining the real musical culture right now. And I haven't heard any Fred Again or Ren at an audio show.
I probably would hear it at IFA, and I think it's because IFA represents companies who understand that they are part of consumer culture. I think the hi-fi industry maybe sometimes thinks that consumer culture is a dirty word. I couldn't disagree more. Knowing who your customer is and what appeals to them and being part of their world, that's our responsibility as manufacturers ultimately.
TR: So what do you see music culture as being in 2026? We're in the middle of one of the most interesting times of audio I can think of, where the new audience who grew up on streaming are coming in and going, ‘I want to move beyond this.’ And that is partly behind the vinyl revival with young people really wanting to actively get into that side — but it's also leading us in the direction of every device having streaming built in or being ‘active’. There are these two arguably separate paths, so where can you ‘meet’ music culture as a company?
CH: There's a little bit of convenience going on here. Active is clearly a future direction for our industry, fueled by convenience and simplicity. I've spent a long time in my career involved in separates hi-fi, and that has a place, but I think even companies who have been focused on that over the last few decades realize that active is the direction of travel. I think that's down to people just wanting a simpler life.
But then there's the ironic flip side of that. We talk about the vinyl revival and analog renaissance and all these things, [including] CDs. I'm using one of my old Motorola phones for my phone because I don't always want to be connected on a smartphone.
But one of my favorite cartoons is [the one that asks] ‘What got you into vinyl? Was it the inconvenience or the expense?’ You know that one? I think the ritual [of playing and choosing vinyl] is really important.
Just for a second, I'm going to kind of dive off into part of how we'll execute our mission. You know, moving into being more a part of music culture isn't just about understanding the music side of it, it's actually how people experience music. I think as an industry, the hi-fi industry has long lamented the question: how do we get people to come in and listen to what music should sound like?
I don't believe [getting people to come to us] is the right answer. Go to where people are listening to music and show them how it could sound. There is a bar culture called the kissa bar culture that came out of Tokyo over the last 20 or so years. It manifests itself in these listening rooms, and you see them at Studio 180 in London, for example. Spotify has just announced its own version of one of these listening rooms as well. That's where music culture is for me.
There was a great article I was reading the other day where it's basically saying listening rooms like that are the new nightclubs. I thought that was super interesting because it's a place where people just assemble, share a passion of music. They might be sipping nice teas or drinking great whiskey or maybe just chatting, you know? It's a place to socialize.
We're seeing this resurgence of gaming, and I mean board gaming. I think that's beautiful, because it's people coming together and escaping the distractions of modern-day technology. It's definitely a younger audience who are doing that because they are sick to the high teeth of everything being online, everything being intangible and losing that connection with friends.
You're seeing it also manifesting in things like running clubs appearing and becoming a huge thing for people in their teens and 20s and early 30s, just craving for human connection.
And I think that is part of music culture. It's human connection. It's why gig tickets are going through the roof again — Glastonbury's selling out faster than ever.
And people really spend more on music, on a hi-fi system or an audio system. They're quite happy with their [premium] Apple Bluetooth products, they're already spending that money. They're dropping £1,000 on Glastonbury tickets and spending all this money on Taylor Swift to get the eight different versions of an album that she releases. They're obsessed by music, but they don't know who to talk to because no one's talking to them.
TR: This might tie back to what your plan is to get out there and interact with people, but the immediate problem that occurs to me with having more of these spaces — and about these spaces becoming more popular even though there's appetite for them — is the general collapse in the ‘third-place’ concept. Places you can go that are not work and that are not home and that are also sustainable businesses. A lot of these places are struggling. Board game cafes have done all right, but you've got maybe one or two per city. They're not like how pubs and bars have been absolutely everywhere in the past. So do you see yourselves opening some of these venues, or supporting them directly in other ways?
CH: I think the pub reference is interesting because we've seen a decline in pubs. We know how many pubs are shutting every week, and nightclubs. I think it's just a different way of people getting together. I'm not surprised that there's only one or two [board game cafes] in a town, because there's probably only ever been one or two nightclubs in a town. Clearly not the same number of people going through [board game cafes as nightclubs], but it's just a place where people can get together.
But just because they're not doing it publicly, doesn't mean they're not doing it at home, you know? We know that vinyl and turntable sales continue to increase year over year over year because people are creating their own environments at home.
In terms of how we execute it, it's by working through our relationships that we have as a team — and that I bring to the business as well in terms of relationships in the music industry and venues within the music industry — and saying ‘how do we support you creating your own listening bar environments’ or being able to [develop] kissa bar culture.
And doing that globally, importantly, as well. We might be based in the UK and proudly British hi-fi brands, but we're a global business, so how do we get a venue in Tokyo, the home of all of this culture? We've had some really good conversations in Vienna just last week about being able to do this in places in Australia, and opportunities in places like New York and across Europe. Spain, Italy and France are way ahead of the UK when it comes to this listening bar culture already.
And then obviously in the UK, our approach will be to support those venues either by equipping them with the right kind of technology to be able to deliver it, or helping people to open them. There's a difference between pop-up events, which are fun for the industry, and actually supporting these venues to be successful in what they're trying to do.
There's an ethical story here. Sometimes people say, ‘So what is it you do as a business? You're making stuff?’ I'm like: no, it's bigger than that. We make products for sure, but they transform people's lives.
It sounds very floaty and you know, almost ephemeral, but it's true: music changes how people feel, so we have a responsibility to make that available to people wherever they want to be. That's kind of our cultural thing, and we'll do that by making sure that the great kit that we make is in the places they want to go to — the two come together.
The outcome is that people realize that [our brands are] actually part of music culture, and therefore we are the people who are signposting who they could listen to great music through, and that's the business upside of it.
TR: So when you talk to these places about what support they need from you, what are they saying?
CH: Support financially. Equipment. There are some which have been really successful with very advanced audio systems, but most locations can't manage that.
We are proudly in the accessible end of the spectrum as a company, particularly around the Q Acoustics range. It's high-quality equipment, but it doesn't cost the Earth, so we can help some of these smaller venues perhaps be part of this movement; we can loan equipment to them, or work with them on [cost]. I think that's probably the practical thing that we'd be able to do.
TR: You’re talking about getting closer to music culture and being a music-listening brand, not a technical brand, if you think of it in those terms. Do you think that's something that separates you from the Chinese hi-fi brands that are exploding in popularity? A lot of them feel quite led by technical people who are able to create pretty incredible products for low prices, but the pitch feels based on technical specs.
CH: I think these brands aren’t that different to traditional hi-fi companies. You know, I've worked in a number of brands where it’s an engineering-led culture — and there's a bit of a transformation that we'll do at Armour Home; there's a degree of engineering-led culture [there].
What has been fun is seeing everything from the engineering teams, but also that our designers saying, ‘Hang on, we could be bolder and braver and less safe and actually be really exciting.’
So I'm already seeing renders for products that will come out in the next 12 to 18 months where I'm like, ‘Yeah, OK, now we're talking’. These are products that really speak to having a sense of style and presence, and really selective decisions around the colors, materials and finishes that we use, and being much closer to interior design. Pantone colors of the year and these similar cultural cues that matter [to people] — just being cool and relevant, that alone is more than maybe the Chinese brands are able to do because they're not attuned to it in quite the same way.
There is a distinction, though. It isn't just British tastes that matter; it's understanding the global tastes as well. So working with our global distributors as well to really get a sense of what is current right now in China or in Australia or in the US, and bringing that as a bit of a mix. Otherwise we fall into the trap I think British hi-fi brands have done in the past where they think everything starts and stops at the English Channel.
TR: Right now, Goldring is really a turntable accessories company that happens to make one turntable [the Goldring GR3]. So, is your plan to expand its reach by offering more turntable models, or are you thinking more about expanding the kind of accessories it makes into phono stages or something else that's not in the range at the moment?
CH: One of my observations when joining the Armour Home Group is that we focus a lot around the Q Acoustics business. And then we have two other businesses within it, which are Goldring and QED. I think that focus is a miss, [and] that's a shame, because we have 120 years this year of history with Goldring. It is one of two of the oldest audio brands in existence, and it has been there at all the defining moments over a century.
Then we have QED, which is 53 years old this year, and it was the brand that started the whole cable revolution from bell wire to proper audio hi-fi grade cables. Something called the Genesis report, which was written by the guys at QED, is still the bible that everyone else has followed ever since.
Q Acoustics has been the new kid on the block a little bit. It's 20 years old this year, so I kind of joke with people in the business that it's not a teenager anymore, we're a grown-up… but we have 120 years of Goldring.
So in the context of your question, Goldring is a beautiful thing for us to have in the family because it allows us to talk about 120 years of history, and iconic decks like the G99 or GL75 with Lenco that were built over the decades. But it's also bang up to date, because vinyl culture is hot.
So we have to do a couple of things. One is to celebrate the past and then also bring things bang up to date in the future. I've had some extraordinary conversations with some of the people I've met in this business, but one of them in particular is a guy called David Giffin.
He's been in the business for 40 years, his father was in the business for 41 years before that, and he was sharing with me this extraordinary scrapbook of all of the sort of cuttings over decades of this business.
That is extraordinary in itself, but he's now the person that people come to from all of the forums going, ‘This is the guy who can rebuild whatever cartridges from around the world’. He's showing me pictures of some Japanese cartridges, like super-esoteric cartridges made out of marble, that he's been tasked with repairing.
So this extraordinary level of skill sits in our Goldring team, and we don't talk about that nearly enough; it's extraordinary. How do we make that manifest itself in the consumer world? We let people know that we have some of the best cartridges, certainly for consistency of performance, that money can buy. We've got everything from entry level right up to Ethos at the top level
You can come to us for turntables too. We have GR3 as a turntable at the moment, and without giving any secrets away, of course we're looking at what more we can do more around that.
But I need to make sure that [a new] turntable is something truly iconic that celebrates 120 years of Goldring, that reminds everybody that this was the brand that started it all, and can sit proudly in a kissa bar environment, celebrated on this plinth, almost like they're shrines. Something that's truly special.
And then at the same time, [should] tie our brands together, so I can use QED technology in the development of that turntable, and I can also make sure we've got Q Acoustic speakers that do service to a turntable with 120 years' worth of history. That’s where some of these new flagship projects that we're working on are really exciting, because the material choices alone are bold.
I talk a lot internally about the thread between the brands. They're not disparate brands. We're incredibly fortunate to have three brands that bring everything together from the source through the connectivity through to the output, and we need to do more of that.
TR: So we should probably expect a cohesive, very premium, very celebratory set of stuff to come from this thinking?
CH: This is where I get kicked under the table by my PR handlers. You should expect a much more bold and confident view as to what we bring to market because I believe we've earned that over many, many, many, many decades.
TR: Are you considering doing something like special edition versions of Q Acoustics speakers that are Goldring-branded or designed? Q Acoustics' design language tends to have friendly, rounded corners, and rounded edges. I look at the GR3 and I see this stark, hard-edged cuboid block. Do you want a set of Q Acoustics speakers that are equally hard-edged and glossy-finished, [and] maybe have the Goldring logo on?
CH: I think it could be that way, or it could be the other way around. You could see a Goldring turntable that leans more into the home-friendly design, or I could see everything elevating to a new design approach as well, sure.
What I can be clearer about is that I think it's important that there are technology linkages where possible across the three brands, and design cues where appropriate across all three as well, without betraying the core design fundamentals of each brand. It's a balancing act.
TR: The biggest missing pieces of your portfolio are the amp and streamer. Is that something you think about expanding into, or do you think the future is more in the combined active speaker route in the Q Acoustics range?
CH: There are two parts to that. We have our core business, and we have our distribution business in the UK, and it’s important to mention that our distribution business is really interesting.
We've got Xgimi at one end in terms of cutting-edge projector technology; we’re just rolling that out with retailers across the UK, and we literally can't keep up with demand.
Almost at the other extreme we've got Grado. Cool as hell, legit New York vibes, super interesting, iconic design. And then in the middle we've got Burson Audio, a head-fi and amp brand.
But there is the missing link [in our brands], which is amplification and streaming. Active speakers definitely support that, clearly, but we have a very successful passive speaker range, and I need to work out how to tackle that. Is that through partnerships? Is that through collaboration with existing manufacturers in the industry, those who are on the same mission as us of understanding that music culture is really important for the industry? Or do we treat it as a distribution opportunity for us in the UK? And I don't have the answer yet, but I know it's important.
TR: QED is surely the hardest brand here to expand beyond the core hi-fi community, unless you take a bit of a left turn. So what is your thinking there? Would you keep QED as a nice ‘glue’ option to connect everything together, or is there some future for QED that goes beyond what it does now?
CH: I would start by saying it’s about re-remembering that QED is the brand that started it all, and helping that awareness grow. There are other brands out there who've established a strong position in the premium and luxury cable sector, but they're all essentially going back to the Genesis report.
We are working on redefining the ranges, I'll put it that way, so you'll see some news coming out of QED fairly soon anyway.
I think connectivity is a question in itself. Cables were the original connection, but now wireless is a connection, and so I'm certainly pondering in my idle moments about whether QED should be in that wireless area. Because it's the modern day glue, and it's interesting you ask the question because it's definitely in my mind.
TR: You alluded to this earlier, but it's the old business study question of asking ‘What do we actually sell? Is it cables or is it connections? And if it's connections, then should we think about something medium than cables in the future?’ Is that the kind of question you're exploring for QED?
CH: Absolutely. And I’m only four weeks in, which is why I'm not giving you clear answers, but I can see that there is a clear consumer understanding among those who know us today that we are the connection. But there are consumers today who don't even know us, they're not being signposted well enough because of the music culture topic we've gone into as to how they listen to music — so they might recognize QED as being the connection, but they're only used to wireless connectivity. And so what do we do with that?
TR: I'm sure you are not going to have anything specific to say on this subject when it comes to products, but it's very relevant to this topic: have you seen the Pro-ject Wireless Box E? They've made this little box that connects directly to the speaker posts on the back of your passive speakers, it plugs into power, and it makes them wireless using the WiiM platform.
CH: I think that's actually quite exciting for our category. A theory I have is that a lot of people are starting to inherit hi-fi, so family members might be getting to an age or passing on, sadly, and people are discovering turntables in the loft. ‘What do I do with this?’
That's interesting for me as well, which is getting people on a journey. One of the companies I worked at was world-famous for understanding the importance of being there at the beginning of someone's journey and being with them for life. It’s a separates company, and it's the upgrade journey that people went on that's really important to me. It's one of the things that I'm talking to the marketing teams about, within the group. It's about making it easier to understand where you start and where you could go.
QED is a perfect example actually, where it's a bit of a maze and really hard to navigate, so making sure that, just from a packaging and a communications point of view, people know where they are on that journey. Are they at the beginning? Are they at our ‘good’, our ‘better’ or our ‘best’ — so they can work out where they could step up through their audio life.
I don't think we have done that enough in our ranges. It's the same with our 3000 series to our 5000 series range, and then up to our Concept portfolio, in Q Acoustics. It's making it really clear about what this [product] does at this level, what you can expect at this [higher] level and what you can expect at this [highest] level. This idea that it's always a little itch that's not quite scratched; it could always get better.
TR: One of the entry points that I think we're seeing a lot of at the moment is desktop speakers. You guys have compact speakers, bookshelf speakers that are pretty small — but in particular, there's this kind of breakout sector right now that’s one step down in size from there. Quite often wireless or active, but designed for people who are getting into the audiophile stage via their desktop. Based on what you were just saying, are you guys exploring more of these opportunities where there is some breakout sector where you can say ‘OK, this is where we can get people on board in our journey’?
CH: I'm gonna half answer that. We have three different bookshelves in our 3000 series and the same in the 5000 series, and those are to meet the needs of three different kinds of bookshelf customer. Some of them are international, like the 3030c, because they’re the bigger of the lot and the US buyers like a larger volume for the cabinet.
The 3010 and 5010 are our small footprint version. They are used in home offices a lot, but I think there are new audiences coming through. There's gaming, and there are younger consumers who might be in flat shares or whatever that need something smaller. So yes, we are watching that part of the industry very closely.
TR: We’ve talked a lot about music, and that's kind of clearly where your focus is as far as building a new identity and the opportunities. But Q Acoustics has such a successful history in the home theater space; it was one of the earliest pioneers of soundbars and soundbases, but left that area really right as it was exploding — though exploding with entries from the likes of LG and Samsung. At the moment, there's no a product in that area; is that something you could see the brand getting back into, or do you want to focus on that music side?
CH: So there is a crossover. Being part of music culture doesn't mean it's exclusive to other elements of it, and I think home entertainment and AV is still very much part of that culture of entertainment. And it is important to us strategically; we still have products in the range that allow us to satisfy a lot of those needs. We have a range of subwoofers from entry through to high performance.
In terms of the soundbar category, it’s quite a scary category. It's very hard to compete with free, and the TV manufacturers will offer a soundbar as free, or give a retailer the latitude to offer it for free to close a TV sale.
I've been actively involved in some products in that space in the past, and I've seen how successful they can be if they are designed really well.
I'm dancing around an answer to say: no plans at the moment. It is a category that I look at with curiosity, but I'm not sure if it's the absolute priority yet. Surround sound, yes — but soundbar, I'm not sure yet.
TR: In surround sound, what we’re seeing there is, again, a lot of people who are ready to step up, in the same way as we talked about people in hi-fi wanting to move up in the journey. One of the key trends happening in home theater right now is the move to wireless surround systems. Do you think that is a route you can see Q Acoustics going down? It's a complicated technical thing to deal with, but I feel like it's something that any company in the space right now needs to reckon with.
CH: So we've definitely got the capabilities to develop solutions in that space. An area we haven't talked about is install, and I think there is a bigger opportunity actually about making install an option for homeowners. We have a branch of products that we call ‘easy install’ — the name says it all, you know, super easy for the average DIYer through to electricians to install. I see that there's probably a future for much more there, in terms of in-ceiling speakers and maybe some satellite speakers to create this environment.
There's a whole tangent we could go down about whether Atmos has gained momentum. I think for me, it's still a ‘watch and see’.
But I think the idea of in-ceiling or in-wall speakers and satellite speakers, and maybe some floorstanders or bookshelves as an option, and them all working together, that's interesting — and I think wireless within that environment is really interesting. And by ‘interesting’ that means ‘yes, I'm considering that’.
The ‘easy install’ stuff is super interesting though for us, because we've all been in this industry a long time. We've seen that installation systems are seen as complex and scary and difficult and expensive. You need a server-mounted system and you need specialisms and you need lots of complexity and disruption to your home… it isn't like that anymore. I've been really blown away.
My wife doesn't know this yet, but I'm going to switch stuff out in our house, because I've suddenly realized how easy it is. Q Acoustics has a thing called the E300a, which is essentially a built-in amplifier and streaming modules in a down-lighter-like size. Wire it up to a couple of in-ceiling speakers, you've got a system ready to go. It couldn't be easier. Voice controlled, so you can say ‘Alexa play BBC 6 Music’ or whatever.
I don't think people realize they can do this yet generally, and that they can do it themselves on a weekend, or they can get their local electrician to come and pop it in, because it's easy. And we're trying to support the electrician channel to do more of that. Maybe that's more interesting than the soundbars on their own.
Let's get nerdyish for a second. HDMI ARC I think is really, really important. Thank God for it, because I think particularly if you're earlier on in your [hi-fi] journey, you have to make some compromises, but you can enjoy hi-fi quality sound through an HDMI ARC interface and it'll still be part of a pseudo AV system.
Sure, it's compromised because you're not going to get the bells and whistles coming from all around — Titanic isn't going to sound quite the same — but it's going to sound beautiful when you listen to music. In that kind of relationship between ‘is it music’ or ‘is it audiovisual’, I think it’s entertainment as a whole, and finding the best of both worlds. HDMI ARC has been a savior.
TR: There's also the element where, if people go to [the] Reddit home theater community for their advice on whether to buy a soundbar, or which is the right soundbar, what they will get is a lot of people saying that they should actually get a stereo setup. There are people who say this will always be better than any soundbar, and you guys do have that option in your active speakers.
CH: That's what I mean; you can get the best of both worlds. That stereo presence though is always going to be better; that’s the point, isn't it, because you're not compromised by [having] the bar in the middle.
TR: So finally, what is the holistic brand proposition you want to offer from Armour Home? If you're addressing what you want all of your brands to do at once, and you’ve got this idea of how you can integrate with the community, what do you want people to think about Q Acoustics and QED and Goldring in combination?
CH: I want people to see that there is a relationship between all three brands that takes us from the origins of the audio experience right up to the modern day. That there is some confidence in those brands, that we understand the legacy that they bring, and that Q Acoustics kind of brings that freshness to it as well.
That we can bring those technologies together more, so there's more integration there and the design and feel about them having a relationship closer together as well. So rather than Armor Home as a parent company being a collection of brands, Armor Home is the home of source through to the output.
And that we've got a vibe as well, that we're not passive, forgive the pun, in this industry — that we recognize that it's about the hairs on your arms. It isn't just about the engineering.
It's just about having a shared passion and experience and being visible to everybody in the places that they enjoy being. This idea of ‘we'll come to you, you don't need to come to us because we are the same as you’.

Matt is TechRadar's Managing Editor for Entertainment, meaning he's in charge of persuading our team of writers and reviewers to watch the latest TV shows and movies on gorgeous TVs and listen to fantastic speakers and headphones. It's a tough task, as you can imagine. Matt has over a decade of experience in tech publishing, and previously ran the TV & audio coverage for our colleagues at T3.com, and before that he edited T3 magazine. During his career, he's also contributed to places as varied as Creative Bloq, PC Gamer, PetsRadar, MacLife, and Edge. TV and movie nerdism is his speciality, and he goes to the cinema three times a week. He's always happy to explain the virtues of Dolby Vision over a drink, but he might need to use props, like he's explaining the offside rule.

articles.title: WhatsApp prueba los contadores de visualizaciones en canales: así sabrás cuántas personas leen tus mensajes
articles.text:
WhatsApp sigue apostando por mejorar la experiencia de comunicación en sus canales y ahora ha comenzado a probar una función esperada por administradores y creadores de contenido: los contadores de visualizaciones en actualizaciones de canal.
Este desarrollo, que lleva más de un año en pruebas, de acuerdo con WABetaInfo, permitirá medir cuántas personas han visto cada publicación, ofreciendo a los administradores una herramienta clave para entender el alcance real de sus mensajes.
PUBLICIDAD
En un entorno donde los canales de WhatsApp se han convertido en una vía esencial para empresas, medios y comunidades, saber qué mensajes logran captar la atención es fundamental para ajustar estrategias, mejorar el contenido y fortalecer la conexión con los seguidores.
Así funcionan los nuevos contadores de visualizaciones
La función, disponible actualmente para algunos evaluadores beta en Android y iOS, muestra a los administradores la cantidad exacta de visualizaciones que recibe cada actualización directamente en la burbuja del mensaje. A medida que los seguidores abren y leen la publicación, el número se actualiza en tiempo real, proporcionando una métrica precisa y actualizada.
PUBLICIDAD
Es importante destacar que este contador es privado: solo el administrador del canal puede verlo. Los seguidores, por ahora, no tienen acceso a estos datos y siguen viendo las actualizaciones de manera habitual, sin indicadores de visualización.
¿Por qué son útiles estos contadores para los administradores?
Los contadores de visualizaciones representan mucho más que una simple estadística. Permiten identificar qué tipo de contenido genera mayor interés, cuáles publicaciones pasan desapercibidas y ayudan a detectar patrones de comportamiento en la audiencia. Con esta información, los administradores pueden adaptar sus estrategias, optimizar la frecuencia de las publicaciones y centrarse en los temas que realmente conectan con sus seguidores.
PUBLICIDAD
Por ejemplo, si una actualización sobre un nuevo producto recibe el doble de visualizaciones que un aviso general, el administrador puede priorizar ese tipo de contenido en el futuro. Con el tiempo, el análisis de estas métricas facilitará la construcción de comunidades más activas y comprometidas.
Contadores públicos: la próxima frontera en WhatsApp
Además de los contadores privados que ya se están desplegando, WhatsApp trabaja en una versión pública de la función. Esta opción permitiría que todos los seguidores de un canal vean cuántas veces se ha visualizado cada publicación, de modo similar a lo que ocurre en otras plataformas sociales.
PUBLICIDAD
La diferencia principal entre el contador privado y el público radica en el acceso a la información: en el modelo actual, solo los administradores ven los datos, mientras que con la versión pública, todos los seguidores podrían identificar rápidamente qué mensajes han tenido mayor alcance o impacto.
Disponibilidad y despliegue de la función
Por el momento, los contadores de visualizaciones privados están disponibles para un grupo reducido de usuarios beta en las últimas versiones de WhatsApp para Android y iOS. Algunos usuarios en la versión estable también pueden tener acceso, pero el despliegue es gradual. Si aún no aparece en tu canal, es cuestión de tiempo: WhatsApp irá ampliando la función a más cuentas en las próximas semanas o meses.
PUBLICIDAD
La empresa no ha anunciado una fecha específica para el lanzamiento global de los contadores, pero la tendencia indica que se convertirán en una herramienta estándar dentro del ecosistema de canales.
Cómo usar la beta de WhatsApp en Android y iOS: proceso paso a paso
Android
- Abre la Google Play Store y busca “WhatsApp”.
- Desplázate hacia abajo en la página de la aplicación hasta encontrar la sección del programa beta.
- Pulsa en “Unirse” si hay cupos disponibles.
- También puedes revisar en la app de WhatsApp: ve a Ajustes > Acceso anticipado a las funciones para activar la beta si tu cuenta lo permite.
- Espera unos minutos y luego actualiza la aplicación para recibir la versión de prueba beta.
iOS (iPhone)
- Descarga e instala la app TestFlight desde la App Store.
- Accede al enlace público de invitación a WhatsApp Beta desde el navegador de tu iPhone.
- Pulsa en “Empezar a probar” para aceptar el cupo dentro de TestFlight (los cupos suelen ser limitados).
- Actualiza WhatsApp a la versión beta desde la misma interfaz de TestFlight.
Nota: Los cupos para el programa beta son limitados y pueden llenarse rápidamente. Si no hay espacio disponible, deberás intentarlo más adelante.
A medida que la función se extienda a todos los usuarios, marcará un nuevo estándar para la interacción y el análisis en la plataforma de mensajería más utilizada del mundo.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Les indispensables de l'été via Cdiscount : 5 essentiels à ne pas oublier avant de partir
articles.text:
Les indispensables de l'été via Cdiscount : 5 essentiels à ne pas oublier avant de partir
Entre les longues journées à la plage, les trajets en voiture et les soirées qui traînent dehors, l'été a ses propres exigences côté équipement. Voici cinq produits qui répondent chacun à un besoin très concret de la saison, de la lecture au soleil à l'organisation de la valise, tous actuellement en promotion chez Cdiscount.
Liseuse Amazon Kindle 16 Go, pour lire sans que l'écran ne chauffe au soleil
Contrairement à une tablette ou un smartphone, l'écran à encre électronique d'une liseuse ne reflète pas la lumière du jour et reste parfaitement lisible en plein soleil, sur une serviette de plage comme en terrasse. Cette Kindle 16 Go, l'entrée de gamme actuelle d'Amazon, embarque un écran de 6 pouces et suffisamment de stockage pour emporter plusieurs centaines de livres sans avoir à faire de tri avant de partir. Sa batterie tient plusieurs semaines en usage normal, de quoi passer l'intégralité d'un séjour sans avoir à penser au chargeur, et la connectique USB-C simplifie la recharge quand elle finit par arriver à court d'autonomie. Autant dire qu’il s’agit là d’un compagnon de vacances qui a l'avantage de ne pas donner envie de vérifier ses notifications toutes les cinq minutes. La liseuse est actuellement proposée à 119,99 €.
Batterie externe NOSHEIR 10 000 mAh, la sécurité en toute circonstance
Entre le GPS qui tourne en continu sur la route des vacances et les photos prises toute la journée, la batterie d'un smartphone ne suit pas toujours le rythme estival. Cette batterie externe de 10 000 mAh, compatible iPhone, Samsung ou Xiaomi, embarque une charge rapide USB-C 3A et surtout un câble intégré directement dans le boîtier, ce qui sera bien pratique pour ne pas avoir à fouiller le fond d'un sac à la recherche du bon cordon. Un écran numérique affiche le niveau de charge restant en temps réel, pour savoir d'un coup d'œil s'il reste de quoi tenir jusqu'au soir. Elle passe de 19,99 € à 15,99 € pendant l'opération, ce qui en fait une petite dépense pour éviter la panne de batterie au pire moment.
Ventilateur brumisateur QUMOX, la fraîcheur portable
Il n’aura échappé à aucune personne clairvoyante que l’été, et surtout cet été 2026, il fait chaud. Pour les épisodes de forte chaleur, ce ventilateur brumisateur portable de QUMOX combine ventilation et fine brumisation d'eau pour un effet rafraîchissant plus marqué qu'un simple ventilateur de poche. Rechargeable par USB et pliable, il se glisse facilement dans un sac sans prendre de place, avec un choix de trois vitesses selon l'intensité recherchée et un affichage numérique du niveau de batterie restant. Parce que parfois, il vaut mieux transformer une attente en plein soleil, un trajet en voiture sans climatisation ou une soirée sur un balcon en moment nettement plus supportable, cet appareil passe de 28 € à 21,99 €.
Casque à conduction osseuse Shokz OpenRun Pro 2, le sport sans s'isoler
Plutôt que de recouvrir l'oreille comme des écouteurs classiques, l'OpenRun Pro 2 de Shokz transmet le son par vibration osseuse au niveau des tempes, en laissant le conduit auditif totalement libre. Ce choix prend d’ailleurs tout son sens en extérieur l'été : courir en gardant la conscience de la circulation autour de soi, faire du vélo sans s'isoler du bruit ambiant, ou simplement garder une oreille sur ce qui se passe à la piscine pendant que l'autre écoute un podcast, voilà tout ce que permet cet appareil. Du reste, le casque revendique 12 heures d'autonomie et repose sur le Bluetooth 5.3 pour une connexion stable avec le smartphone. Il passe de 199 € à 134,99 € pendant la promotion : c’est là une réduction notable sur un modèle qui reste une référence dans sa catégorie.
Sac de voyage à compression sous vide Travel Scenery, pour mieux optimiser sa valise
Dernier indispensable, ce sac de voyage à compression sous vide de la marque Travel Scenery mise sur un principe simple : celui de réduire le volume des vêtements en chassant l'air à l'intérieur des poches dédiées, pour gagner de la place dans un bagage déjà plein. Avec ses dimensions de 47 x 33 x 20 cm, il reste compatible avec les formats de bagage cabine, tout en offrant 35 litres de contenance grâce à ses nombreuses poches et sa conception imperméable. Voilà qui sera bien utile pour isoler du linge humide (comme, au hasard, des serviettes de plage) ou protéger le contenu d'une averse impromptue. C’est une solution particulièrement adaptée à qui voyage léger côté bagages mais chargé côté affaires à emporter. Il passe de 109,99 € à 45,99 €, soit la remise la plus importante de cette sélection.

articles.title: Feux de forêt en Gironde : quand les cartes générées par IA alimentent la panique
articles.text:
Alors que l’incendie parti de Saumos a parcouru plusieurs dizaines de milliers d’hectares, les cartes se multiplient sur les réseaux sociaux. Elles ne montrent pourtant pas toutes la même chose et certaines peuvent donner une vision très trompeuse de la situation, parfois jusqu'à semer la panique.
L’incendie qui touche la Gironde depuis le 22 juillet est désormais « stabilisé », mais pas encore « fixé », a indiqué le ministre de l’Intérieur Laurent Nuñez ce lundi 27 juillet. Environ 42 000 hectares ont été parcourus par le feu et 220 000 personnes ont fait l’objet d’une évacuation préventive depuis le début de la crise.
Face à un événement d'une telle ampleur, le réflexe est compréhensible : ouvrir les réseaux sociaux pour s'informer, et consulter une carte pour savoir où se trouvent les flammes et si elles se rapprochent d'une commune ou d'une habitation. Mais les réseaux sociaux regorgent d'images de fiabilité très inégale : captures de services satellites, cartes météorologiques, tracés d'internautes et, plus inquiétant, des cartes générées par intelligence artificielle qui exagèrent délibérément l'étendue du sinistre. Certaines sont donc entièrement fabriquées. Et même celles qui reposent sur des données réelles peuvent devenir trompeuses lorsqu'elles sont périmées, sorties de leur contexte ou accompagnées d'une mauvaise légende.
Une carte des zones brûlées ne montre pas nécessairement où se trouve le feu
L’incendie de Saumos en fournit une bonne démonstration. Sa progression, son intensité et son orientation ont évolué plusieurs fois en quelques jours, au gré du vent, de l’humidité et des reprises de feu. Une capture réalisée le matin peut donc être très éloignée de la situation observée quelques heures plus tard.
Il faut surtout déterminer ce que la carte prétend représenter. Un périmètre de 42 000 hectares correspond à une surface parcourue par l’incendie. Cela ne signifie pas que l’ensemble de cette zone est simultanément recouvert de flammes, ni que tous ses points présentent le même niveau de danger.
La confusion est également fréquente avec les cartes de vigilance. La Météo des forêts indique le niveau de risque de départ et de propagation d’un incendie pour chaque département. La carte de la Défense des forêts contre les incendies d’Aquitaine renseigne quant à elle sur les restrictions d’accès et de circulation dans les massifs. Ces outils sont essentiels pour la prévention, mais ils ne localisent pas les fronts de flammes en temps réel.
Une zone colorée en rouge ou en noir peut ainsi signaler un risque extrême ou une interdiction d’accès, sans qu’un incendie y soit actuellement actif. À l’inverse, une zone déjà brûlée peut rester visible sur une carte alors que le front principal s’est déplacé.
Pour les personnes directement menacées, les cartes ne doivent jamais remplacer les instructions de la préfecture, des communes et des services de secours. En Gironde, le dispositif FR-Alert a notamment été déclenché afin d’envoyer directement sur les téléphones l’ordre d’évacuation des populations situées dans les secteurs menacés.
Au Canada comme en Gironde, de fausses cartes ont inventé la position des incendies
Le risque ne se limite toutefois pas à une mauvaise lecture de données authentiques. Des cartes entièrement fabriquées peuvent désormais adopter l’apparence d’un document "crédible".
L’AFP a récemment vérifié plusieurs cartes diffusées pendant les incendies de juillet 2026 au Canada. Générées artificiellement, elles ne provenaient d’aucun service de surveillance reconnu, mais avaient tout de même recueilli des milliers de réactions sur les réseaux sociaux.
L’une d’elles plaçait des symboles de flammes à proximité de Toronto alors que les services officiels de l’Ontario ne recensaient aucun incendie actif dans ce secteur à la date concernée. Une autre reprenait abusivement l’identité visuelle du Centre interservices des feux de forêt du Canada et représentait des foyers sur l’île de Baffin, dans l’Arctique, où aucun feu n’était alors signalé.
Ces images ne se contentaient donc pas de rendre la situation plus spectaculaire. Elles inventaient des foyers, modifiaient leur position et leur attribuaient une fausse source officielle. Certaines ont ensuite été reprises pour alimenter des affirmations complotistes sur l’origine des incendies.
Ces cartes artificielles circulent aussi autour des feux français. Le 25 juillet, une carte présentée comme une "situation en direct" des incendies, revendiquant abusivement des données de Copernicus et des SDIS, a été partagée près de 3 000 fois sur Facebook. Elle affichait des foyers dans des localités introuvables sur aucune carte officielle et un bilan incohérent avec les chiffres des autorités. Le même jour, une infographie générée par intelligence artificielle (et signalée comme telle par la plateforme, sans que cela freine sa diffusion) superposait la carte des incendies à celle des projets photovoltaïques, insinuant un lien entre les deux tout en se défendant d'évoquer un "complot".
Le précédent canadien de juillet 2026 avait déjà montré la mécanique : des cartes inventant des foyers et s'attribuant une fausse source officielle. Chercher les traditionnels défauts graphiques de l'intelligence artificielle ne suffit plus (même s'ils sont évidents dans ces deux exemples). Une carte peut afficher des frontières correctes et des noms parfaitement lisibles tout en reposant sur des données inventées, ou sur des lieux qui n'existent pas.
Ces fausses alertes ne restent pas cantonnées aux fils d'actualité. Ces dernières semaines, les centres d'appel des pompiers ont fait face à une multiplication de sollicitations pour des motifs mineurs (odeur de fumée, ciel voilé, etc.), y compris depuis des secteurs éloignés de tout front actif. Difficile d'attribuer chaque appel à une publication précise : la fumée bien réelle de l'incendie, qui voyage sur des centaines de kilomètres, suffit à inquiéter. Mais des cartes plaçant des foyers imaginaires dans la Sarthe, l'Allier ou la Vienne ne peuvent qu'entretenir cette confusion : un habitant qui découvre une flamme sur la carte "près de chez lui" alors que le feu se trouve à des centaines de kilomètres a toutes les raisons de composer le 18. Chaque appel infondé mobilise un opérateur qui ne traite pas, pendant ce temps, un appel venu d'une zone réellement menacée.
Ce que représentent vraiment les points détectés par satellite
Les cartes de la NASA et du service européen Copernicus constituent des outils beaucoup plus fiables, à condition de bien comprendre leur fonctionnement.
Le système FIRMS de la NASA fournit des informations presque en temps réel à partir des instruments MODIS et VIIRS installés sur plusieurs satellites. Ceux-ci ne photographient pas simplement les flammes : ils recherchent des anomalies thermiques, c’est-à-dire des zones dont la température se distingue nettement de celle des terrains environnants.
MODIS travaille avec des pixels d’environ un kilomètre, contre 375 mètres pour VIIRS. Ce dernier peut donc repérer des foyers plus petits et aider à mieux suivre les grands incendies. Les informations sont normalement actualisées plusieurs fois par jour et intégrées au service européen EFFIS environ deux à trois heures après l’acquisition des images.
Mais un point rouge ne représente pas la surface exacte d’un incendie. Il indique qu’une anomalie thermique a été détectée quelque part dans le pixel concerné. Sa taille à l’écran dépend du mode d’affichage de la carte et ne permet pas de mesurer directement l’étendue des flammes.
Tous les points chauds ne correspondent pas non plus à des feux de forêt. Les satellites peuvent détecter des brûlages agricoles, des installations industrielles ou d’autres sources de chaleur. EFFIS applique des filtres tenant compte de l’occupation des sols, de la proximité des zones urbaines et du degré de confiance de la détection, mais les faux positifs ne peuvent pas être totalement exclus. Des incendies peuvent inversement passer momentanément inaperçus lorsqu’ils sont trop petits ou masqués par les nuages et la fumée.
Avant de partager une carte, quelques vérifications permettent donc d’éviter les erreurs les plus grossières : retrouver sa publication originale, contrôler sa date et son heure, lire sa légende et vérifier si elle représente un risque, une anomalie thermique, un front actif ou un périmètre déjà brûlé.
Une carte sans source identifiable et sans horodatage n’a aucune valeur opérationnelle, aussi spectaculaire soit-elle. La désinformation ne prend d’ailleurs pas toujours la forme d’une image entièrement fabriquée : une vraie carte publiée avec une mauvaise légende ou plusieurs jours trop tard peut être presque aussi trompeuse.
Une anomalie thermique correspond à un pixel satellite dont la signature infrarouge indique une température nettement plus élevée que l’environnement proche. Cela ne “voit” pas forcément une flamme : la détection peut venir d’un feu de végétation, d’un brûlage agricole, d’une activité industrielle ou d’un autre point chaud. Le marqueur affiché sur la carte ne représente pas la surface exacte de l’incendie, mais la présence d’un signal chaud quelque part à l’intérieur du pixel concerné. Les services comme EFFIS appliquent des filtres (occupation des sols, proximité urbaine, niveau de confiance), sans pouvoir éliminer tous les faux positifs. À l’inverse, de petits foyers ou des zones masquées par nuages et fumées peuvent échapper temporairement à la détection.
MODIS et VIIRS sont deux capteurs embarqués sur satellites qui n’ont pas la même résolution au sol : environ 1 km pour MODIS, contre 375 m pour VIIRS. Plus le pixel est grand, plus une détection indique seulement qu’il existe une source chaude quelque part dans une zone étendue, sans permettre de localiser finement le foyer. Avec VIIRS, on peut repérer des foyers plus petits et suivre plus précisément la dynamique d’un grand incendie, mais cela reste une détection « par pixel », pas un tracé exact du front de flammes. La différence de résolution peut aussi expliquer pourquoi deux cartes basées sur des capteurs différents ne “dessinent” pas la même situation. Enfin, la fréquence de passage des satellites et les délais d’intégration des données influencent la “fraîcheur” des points affichés.
La surface parcourue désigne l’emprise totale des zones touchées par le feu depuis le début de l’événement, sans signifier que toute la zone brûle en même temps. Le front actif correspond aux secteurs où l’incendie est en cours de propagation et où l’intensité peut évoluer très vite selon le vent, l’humidité ou les reprises de feu. Une carte de risque (ex. vigilance feux de forêt) ne localise pas un incendie en cours : elle estime la probabilité de départ et de propagation selon les conditions météo et l’état de la végétation. D’autres cartes indiquent des restrictions d’accès (massifs fermés, circulation limitée), ce qui peut être confondu à tort avec une carte de feux actifs. Pour interpréter correctement une carte, il faut identifier précisément ce qu’elle mesure, ainsi que sa date et son heure.

articles.title: Cruciferra Crypter Uses BYOVD and Process Ghosting to Hide Windows Malware
articles.text:
The China-linked cybercrime group behind the use of income tax-related phishing lures targeting Indian taxpayers, tax professionals, and corporate finance teams has been observed using a sophisticated crypter service called Cruciferra.
According to a new analysis by Proofpoint, Cruciferra has been utilized by various unrelated cybercriminal threat clusters to deliver a wide array of remote access trojans (RATs) and information stealer malware.
"Cruciferra is written in Mono and features numerous techniques designed to evade detection, analysis, and incident response efforts," the enterprise security company said in an analysis published last week.
"These include using indirect system calls, API and Import Address Table (IAT) unhooking, bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver (BYOVD)-based EDR tampering, privilege escalation, persistence mechanisms, and a customized implementation of Process Ghosting used to execute payloads while minimizing forensic artifacts."
Crypters (also spelled cryptors) play an important role in the cybercriminal ecosystem as they allow bad actors to obfuscate their payloads, avoid detection, and improve malware delivery success rates.
An emphasis on payload protection notwithstanding, Cruciferra supports various custom encryption routines that appear to be dynamically derived and assembled from established cryptographic algorithms, thereby introducing variations between samples and complicating static analysis as well as signature-based detections.
"The algorithm used to encrypt payloads and strings in each set of samples is different, and there is such a large variance of these algorithms, which means it is probably randomly generated (polymorphically) from elements of well-known hashing, PRNG, and cipher algorithms," per researchers Chris Wakelin, Georgi Mladenov, and Kyle Cucci.
The service has been advertised on the cybercrime underground as the "most lethal crypter" for $450 to $2,000 a month. It was first made available for sale in fall 2025. Some of the commodity malware families distributed via Cruciferra include Agent Tesla, AsyncRAT, DarkCloud Stealer, Formbook, Phantom Stealer, Remcos RAT, Snake Keylogger, ValleyRAT, XLoader, XWorm, and zgRAT.
Campaigns leveraging the crypter have leveraged phishing as the primary initial access vector, with the tool incorporating the flexibility to either drop an encrypted payload to disk or download it from a staging server. The activity is assessed to be opportunistic, reaching anywhere between hundreds and thousands of messages per campaign. The primary targets include financial services, healthcare, government, education, and manufacturing sectors.
One such campaign has been attributed to Chinese-speaking cybercrime actor TA4922, which shares some level of overlap with another prolific threat group called Silver Fox. This involves employing tax-themed lures to drive victims to attacker-controlled landing pages hosting ZIP files to deliver malware. Four such campaigns have been identified between April and early June 2026.
It's worth mentioning here that this attack was documented in detail earlier this month by Seqrite Labs and Cyderes Howler Cell. Seqrite Labs is tracking the activity under the moniker Operation DragonReturn.
Other campaigns that have been observed using Cruciferra are below -
- Emails impersonating the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) to deliver XWorm and AdaptixC2 (May 2026)
- Email using themes related to bed bugs and guest complaints to target organizations in the hospitality and travel industries and deliver zgRAT (late June 2026)
Regardless of the campaign, Cruciferra is always executed via DLL side-loading, while leveraging evasion and anti-analysis techniques to fly under the radar. This includes hiding console windows, unhooking Windows API functions to reduce visibility, indirect system calls, disabling user notifications, and the abuse of the "GoFlyDrv.sys" driver as part of a BYOVD attack to terminate security processes.
"Cruciferra checks if it is running with Administrator privileges, and if not, attempts to elevate its privileges by bypassing UAC using the COM Elevation Moniker," Proofpoint explained. "Additionally, Cruciferra establishes persistence by writing to the registry Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key with a default value of 'putty.' This ensures Cruciferra runs after system reboot."
The final payload is loaded into memory using a variant of Process Ghosting, which, at a high level, refers to an advanced malware evasion technique on Windows where malicious code is executed from a temporary file that is deleted from the disk before the process starts. This, in turn, blinds security products as there is no "file" to scan.
Cruciferra adds an extra layer of sophistication by patching ZwQueryVirtualMemory hooks and by attempting to tamper with the NtManageHotPatch routine to hide the deletion of the file and neutralize integrity checks."While crypters have long been used to evade detection and increase malware delivery and execution success rates, Cruciferra distinguishes itself through its extensive and unique defense-evasion capabilities, modular design, and highly customized and varied approach to payload protection," Proofpoint concluded.

articles.title: I don't think Googlebooks are just Chromebooks — they're a direct shot at Windows
articles.text:
I don't think Googlebooks are just Chromebooks — they're a direct shot at Windows
A whole generation grew up using Chromebooks at school. With AI-first Googlebooks, Google is giving them a reason not to switch to a PC
While OpenAI continues to sit pat on whatever device it is planning to build with Jony Ive, it is embarking on a journey that Google began years ago with the launch of the Android and Chrome OS operating systems followed by its own Pixel devices.
Long before anyone had heard of ChatGPT, Google CEO Sundar Pichai made clear that AI was a primary driver behind Google’s device push. Now, the company’s journey is about to take a turn with the launch of Googlebooks.
While Googlebooks and Chromebooks will coexist for a number of years, it’s clear that the former will eventually replace the latter. But are Googlebooks actually new “books” or really just new “chapters” that represent an evolution of the Chromebook. That depends on where the comparison lies.
Chromebooks have done an excellent job of retaining attributes such as ease of management, security, and affordability. On the other hand, the AI-first mission of the Googlebook represents a dramatic contrast from the cloud-first mission of the Chromebook, and the two platforms carry significant enough differences to justify the new naming.
Foremost, the Googlebooks’ new technical foundation of Android should greatly improve the performance and integration of Android apps versus today’s Chromebooks.
A crash landing from the cloud
Indeed, that serves as a reminder that the original philosophy of the Chromebook as a minimalist web app appliance disappeared a long time ago. And while it is still tough to beat the Chromebook when it comes to computing on a tight budget (Microsoft’s most recent attempt, the education-focused Surface Laptop SE, had the company’s quickest market retreat since Windows RT), Google and its partners have sought to climb the pricing ladder with Chromebook Pluses.
These devices, which have embraced higher quality materials and earlier access to Google’s AI innovations (albeit mostly cloud-based ones), have sold well enough to signal to Google that the market is ready for Windows alternatives that shift away from competing so heavily on price.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
While it’s not a perfect parallel for what Apple was able to do in bringing kids who grew up with the Apple II to the Mac, Google has an opportunity to provide a more capable alternative to a generation of kids who grew up with Chromebooks, particularly at a time when AI stands to transform the PC experience from being a tool to being an agent.
And so the more important question becomes not how Googlebooks will diverge from Chromebooks, but how their new functionality will stack up to Windows, which will also of course continue to evolve.
In this sense, Google’s timing is excellent because it does not need to rely on Android versions of apps catching up to Windows versions; the company has never had much luck getting developers to optimize for Android platforms beyond the phone. Rather, it can compete on a new breed of AI-focused functionality.
But despite Microsoft pulling back from cramming CoPilot into every corner of its desktop operating system, it is still in the early days of integrating AI into that platform as well.
At Build, for example, Microsoft showed not only how it is bringing OpenClaw-pioneered workflows into Windows, but how it is expanding the supporting processor family to include the bold and powerful RTX Spark architecture from MediaTek and Nvidia.
That should put some distance between Windows and Android-based PCs at the top of the market, but the real test will come down to how well Microsoft can scale such AI down versus how well Google scales its desktop AI up.
Ross Rubin is the founder and principal analyst at Reticle Research, a technology research and advisory firm. Ross has been an industry analyst focusing on innovation in products, services, and enabling infrastructure in the tech, media and telecom markets for more than 30 years, writing columns for Engadget, ZDNet, and Fast Company, among other publications. articles.title: Papelera de WhatsApp en Android y iPhone: dónde está y cómo liberar espacio en segundos
articles.text:
WhatsApp, una aplicación usada diariamente para enviar mensajes, imágenes y documentos, incorpora una herramienta específica para evitar que la memoria del teléfono se sature: una papelera de reciclaje integrada en la administración de almacenamiento, accesible desde el menú de configuración.
La función de papelera, presente tanto en Android como en iPhone, ayuda a controlar el almacenamiento ocupado por WhatsApp, ofreciendo una solución directa para quienes buscan mantener el sistema operativo en condiciones óptimas.
PUBLICIDAD
En este sentido, se explican los pasos para liberar espacio que ocupan archivos de WhatsApp en celular, sumado a otras prácticas para evitar que extraños accedan a información que almacena la aplicación como fotos, video y documentos.
Dónde está la papelera de WhatsApp en Android y iPhone
La función conocida popularmente como “papelera de reciclaje” no aparece bajo ese nombre dentro de la aplicación. Se integra en el apartado de Administración de almacenamiento, disponible en el menú de Configuración de la app.
PUBLICIDAD
Tanto en Android como en iPhone, el acceso es similar: se ingresa en Configuración o ajustes y se selecciona Almacenamiento y datos. Dentro de este apartado, WhatsApp muestra una lista detallada de los archivos que ocupan más espacio en el dispositivo, incluyendo imágenes, videos, audios y documentos.
Este desglose facilita la identificación de los elementos prescindibles, permitiendo gestionar cada categoría de forma independiente y sin afectar información esencial de la aplicación.
Cómo realizar la limpieza de archivos desde la papelera de WhatsApp
La visualización de archivos en la sección de Administración de almacenamiento permite seleccionar y eliminar rápidamente aquellos elementos que ya no son necesarios. Es posible revisar cada categoría y elegir los archivos de gran tamaño que ocupan más memoria.
PUBLICIDAD
El sistema indica la cantidad total de espacio usado por cada chat, lo que agiliza la detección de grupos o chats individuales que generan mayor acumulación de archivos.
Esta herramienta es muy útil en dispositivos que reciben un volumen elevado de archivos multimedia, donde la memoria interna puede llenarse en poco tiempo.
Qué impacto tiene la liberación de espacio en el rendimiento del teléfono
Un dispositivo con la memoria saturada experimenta problemas de funcionamiento. El sistema operativo y las aplicaciones requieren espacio libre para generar archivos temporales y gestionar la memoria RAM.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuando el margen de almacenamiento se reduce, el teléfono responde con lentitud y puede registrar cierres inesperados de aplicaciones, sumado a un mayor desgaste de la memoria flash.
WhatsApp puede llegar a ocupar varios gigabytes en dispositivos con uso intensivo, en especial en cuentas activas en múltiples grupos. Mantener el control sobre el espacio ocupado por la aplicación es fundamental para garantizar el rendimiento óptimo del celular y prolongar su vida útil.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuáles pautas de seguridad acompañan la gestión de almacenamiento
La administración del espacio de almacenamiento debe complementarse con prácticas de seguridad sugeridas por WhatsApp, que evitan accesos desautorizados a las cuentas y reducen el riesgo de estafas, robos, fraudes e intentos de suplantación de identidad.
Es esencial activar la verificación en dos pasos desde el menú de configuración en la app de WhatsApp. Esta función añade un código PIN adicional al registrar el número en un nuevo dispositivo, dificultando accesos no autorizados y reduciendo el riesgo de pérdida de información personal.
PUBLICIDAD
Se sugiere mantener la aplicación actualizada, porque cada versión corrige posibles vulnerabilidades y refuerza la seguridad.
Asimismo, es útil revisar periódicamente los dispositivos conectados, accediendo a la sección de Dispositivos vinculados en WhatsApp, cerrando aquellas sesiones que no resulten familiares.
PUBLICIDAD
No compartir el código de verificación recibido por SMS y evitar instalar aplicaciones de origen desconocido son medidas adicionales que contribuyen a que la información y las conversaciones permanezcan protegidas ante intentos de fraude.
